description: How to build and govern artificial intelligence that is fair, transparent, private, safe and accountable: the harms AI systems cause, fairness and bias, transparency and explainability, privacy and data rights, safety and robustness, governance and regulation, and what responsible AI means for African contexts. Taught through browser-based exercises that audit real datasets and models for bias, probe them for failures and apply mitigations, grounding each principle in hands-on measurement rather than theory alone.
modelledOn: Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan, Fairness and Machine Learning
outcomes: Identify and categorise the harms an AI system can cause across its lifecycle.
Measure bias and apply fairness definitions, recognising the trade-offs between them.
Explain model behaviour with interpretability methods and produce transparency documentation.
Protect privacy and uphold data rights when collecting and using data.
Assess and improve the safety and robustness of a model against failures and attacks.
Apply governance frameworks and regulation and adapt responsible-AI practice to African contexts.

units.title: Harms from AI systems
topics: A taxonomy of harms: allocative, representational, quality-of-service, and harms to autonomy and dignity
Where harm enters the lifecycle: problem framing, data, model, deployment and feedback loops
Case studies: biased hiring and credit scoring, flawed facial recognition, content-moderation failures
Harms with regional weight: credit scoring for the unbanked and mobile-money risk models
Stakeholders and the diffusion of responsibility; who bears the cost

units.title: Fairness and bias
topics: Sources of bias: historical, representation, measurement, aggregation and deployment bias
Group fairness definitions: demographic parity, equalised odds, predictive parity
Individual and counterfactual fairness; the impossibility results that force trade-offs
Measuring disparity and auditing a model on a held-out dataset in the browser
Mitigations at pre-processing, in-processing and post-processing stages
Choosing protected attributes sensitively where ethnicity, language and region are involved

units.title: Transparency and explainability
topics: Transparency versus explainability versus interpretability
Intrinsically interpretable models versus post-hoc explanation
Local explanations: feature attribution, LIME and Shapley-value methods
Global explanations, partial-dependence and the limits and misuse of explanations
Documentation: model cards, datasheets for datasets and system fact sheets
Explaining a decision to an affected user such as a declined loan applicant

units.title: Privacy and data rights
topics: Personal data, consent, purpose limitation and data minimisation
Ghana's Data Protection Act 843 and the role of the Data Protection Commission
Re-identification risk and the failure of naive anonymisation
Privacy-preserving techniques: k-anonymity, differential privacy and federated learning in brief
Data collection ethics for low-resource languages and communities; informed consent in practice

units.title: Safety and robustness
topics: Distribution shift and why accuracy on a test set overstates real-world reliability
Adversarial examples and data poisoning; probing a model's brittleness in the browser
Uncertainty estimation, calibration and knowing when to abstain
Robustness to missing data, noisy inputs and intermittent connectivity
Monitoring, drift detection and safe rollback after deployment

units.title: AI governance and regulation
topics: Risk-based governance: the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and an AI management system
The emerging regulatory landscape and risk tiers; sectoral rules for finance and health
Impact assessments, audits and accountability structures within an organisation
Procurement and third-party model risk; responsibility across a supply chain
Standards, voluntary codes and the limits of self-regulation

units.title: AI for African contexts
topics: Data scarcity and representation for African languages, faces and settings
Infrastructure realities: offline and low-bandwidth deployment, on-device models, power cuts
Data sovereignty, benefit sharing and avoiding extractive data practices
Continental and national policy: the African Union's AI stance and local strategy
Building appropriate, locally governed AI rather than importing ill-fitting systems

units.title: A responsible-AI assessment
topics: Combining fairness, transparency, privacy and safety into one evaluation of a system
Producing an impact assessment and a mitigation and monitoring plan
Communicating findings to technical and non-technical stakeholders
Capstone: audit a provided model and dataset and deliver a responsible-AI report with fixes
